title: Far, and near
hookLine: a boy finds God in his own heart, opens his eyes, and finds him standing in front of him
carry: god is far, and god is near

cards: You met Dhruva on day thirteen: the little prince kept off his father's lap, who walked into the forest to find God. Here's the part of his story that belongs to this week.
The Bhagavata Purana says he went so deep in meditation that he saw Vishnu shining in his own heart. Then, suddenly, the form inside him vanished. Dhruva, frightened, opened his eyes.
And there, standing in front of him in the forest, was the same Lord he had been seeing within. Inside, and then outside. The same one.

teach.b: The Isha's verses four and five try to say what Dhruva saw. Verse four: it is one, unmoving, and swifter than the mind; standing still, it outruns those who run. Verse five: tad ejati tan naijati.

teach.h: IT MOVES; IT DOES NOT MOVE.
teach.b: It moves; it does not move. Tad dure tad v antike.
It is far, and it is near. It is inside all this, and outside all this. Why talk in contradictions?

Because any single statement would shrink it. Say God is far away, beyond the stars, and you've made God absent from your kitchen. Say God is only right here, and you've made God small enough to fit on a shelf.
Hindu teaching holds both: Brahman, beyond every name, and the Lord who lives in your heart and answers to a pet name. Later schools read the verses differently.

Shankara's Advaita hears one reality behind every appearance; Ramanuja's line hears a personal Lord living in everything as its inner self, and still more than it. And you can see both in a single Hindu home.
In many families a small murti of baby Krishna, Laddu Gopal, is woken in the morning, bathed, dressed, fed, even given a little sweater in winter.
The same family will tell you Krishna is Lord of the whole universe. That isn't a contradiction they've missed. It's the Isha's verse, lived out: far, and near.
Swifter than the mind, and close enough to tuck in.

how: Many Hindu families care for a small murti of baby Krishna, Laddu Gopal, as a beloved child while worshiping Krishna as Lord of the universe: Isha verse 5's 'far, and near' in one home.

s: the Isha describes the one behind all this with a single clear definition
it gives contradictions on purpose: it moves and doesn't move, far and near.
in the story, the Lord Dhruva saw in front of him was the same one he saw within
the Bhagavata says the form in his heart vanished, and he found it standing before him.
every Hindu school reads these verses the same way
Advaita hears one reality; Ramanuja's school hears a personal Lord indwelling all.

games.q: your little cousin asks: if krishna is lord of the whole universe, why does nani put a sweater on her tiny laddu gopal?
o: it's just a doll; she's being silly.
god is far and near: beyond everything, and close enough to care for.
the universe-god and the baby are two different gods.
games.why: tad dure tad v antike: it is far, and it is near. the Isha refuses to make the Lord only one.

practice: Look out at something vast: the sky through a window, or the thought of the whole earth turning. Let it be far. Then close your eyes and rest a hand on your chest, where Dhruva saw the Lord, and let the same presence be near.
If you pray, say a name of God you love, once for far and once for near. If you don't, just hold both: the very big, and the very close.

wordCard.voice: Ejati, it moves, it stirs. Tad ejati tan naijati: it moves, it does not move; it is far, and it is near, inside all this and outside it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: ejati, it moves, it stirs; verse five: tad ejati tan naijati, it moves, it does not move.

carryVoice: Your line: god is far, and god is near. Dhruva found him inside, then standing in front of him. That's day two hundred thirty-five.
